sections.COMMENTS:
ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
This Source is hypothesised to correspond to a 5-km offshore portion of the Bagnara Calabra-Bovalino Line, a rather obvious tectonic lineament that so far has received very little attention. This line marks the boundary between two portions of the Aspromonte Range: a lower (max elevation is ca. 1,000 m), more slowly uplifting, NNE-trending elongated section locally known as "Dossone della Melia" to the north; and a higher (ca. 2,000 m), faster growing (up to 1.5 mm/y and more), rather circular-shaped block known as "Aspromonte" s.s. (or "Montalto") to the south.
The general NNE trend of local tectonic structures makes a rather sharp right turn as they cross the Bagnara Calabra-Bovalino Line.
The Database hypothesises that, simply based on the macro-observations described above, this is an active lineament characterised by oblique (normal-right lateral) kinematics and mirroring the Nicotera Gioiosa Ionica Line located 25 km to the north. The minimum depth of faulting is set by similarity with the adjacent Gioia Tauro Plain. The maximum depth of faulting is constrained by scaling relationships of width vs. magnitude.
The 16 November 1894 earthquake struck a region straddling the southern end of the Gioia Tauro Plain and the northwestern slope of the Aspromonte proper. The area of largest damage includes a section of the coastline centred between Palmi and Gioia Tauro and the Aspromonte piedmont between Seminara and Oppido. Based on descriptions by contemporary workers (see for example Baratta, 1897), we hypothesise that the 1894 earthquake was in fact composed of clearly separated shocks, one located offshore in front of Palmi, the other located inland about 15 km to the ESE near Delianuova. We also assume that the second (inland) shock was somewhat larger than the first. The two sources are separated by a small source (Aspromonte Northwest) that is assumed to have ruptured in the 1783 sequence (6 February). This Source is associated with the first offshore shock.
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) Was the 1894 really composed of two sub-events? Did the numerous foreshocks occur also on the Bagnara Calabra-Bovalino Line?
2) Is there any more specific evidence for active faulting along the Bagnara Calabra-Bovalino Line?
3) What is the true geometry at depth of this source, and how is it linked with the Gioia Tauro Plain, which is assumed to be a pure normal fault?
sections.SUMMARIES: This source has been established during the research that led to the compilation of this Database. For this reason no specific geological study exists to date concerning its identification, characteristics and seismogenic potential. Nevertheless, this source may have generated a large earthquake in the past. Additional information on the associated earthquake may then be retrieved from the "Catalogue of Strong Earthquakes in Italy (461 B.C.-1997) and Mediterranean Area (760 B.C.-1500)" (Guidoboni et al., 2007), also available from http://storing.ingv.it/cfti4med/.

pictures.t: Kinematic map of the Calabrian Arc
pictures.c: This map shows the strike-slip tectonics of the Calabrian Arc. The Bagnara-Bovalino source is part of the Bagnara Calabra - Bovalino Line, the southernmost major strike-slip lineament of the Calabrian Arc (from Knott and Turco [1991]).

pictures.t: Seismic profiles across the Bovalino strike-slip fault
pictures.c: These two seismic profiles show the flower structure related to the Bagnara Calabra - Bovalino strike-slip Line. In the Ionian offshore this structure shows transpressive kinematics (from Del Ben et al. [2008]).

Ghisetti [1984] describes both the Gioia Tauro Plain and the Upper Mesima basins as two graben formed by main west-dipping and secondary east-dipping faults, and points out the existence of transverse structures separating individual basins.
Schematic section of the fault systems in the general context of the active Calabrian W-dipping subduction (from Tiberti et al. [2017]).
